young.html: Five hundred years ago, many Christians in Europe were arguing about what the Church should teach and how it should be run. This time is called the Reformation. One of its leaders was a young Frenchman named John Calvin.

When Calvin was only 26, he wrote a book to explain, clearly and in order, what he believed the Bible teaches. He called it the Institutes of the Christian Religion. "Institutes" meant "instruction": a teaching book. He kept making it bigger and better for the rest of his life.

Calvin lived and worked in the city of Geneva, in Switzerland. His ideas spread to Scotland, the Netherlands, France and England, and later across the ocean with the Pilgrims and Puritans to America. Churches that follow his teaching are often called Reformed or Presbyterian.

young.html: Make a table of contents. Calvin organized his whole book in four parts, following an old Christian statement of belief called the Apostles' Creed. Pick something you know a lot about (a sport, a game, a hobby) and plan a book about it in four parts. What comes first? What comes last? Why?

full.html: John Calvin (1509–1564) was born in Noyon, in northern France, studied law and the humanist classics, and around 1533 joined the movement for reform begun by Martin Luther. Protestants were being persecuted in France, so he left. In 1536, in Basel, he published the first Institutes, six chapters long, with a preface asking King Francis I to stop the persecution. That same year he was persuaded to stay in Geneva, and apart from a few years in Strasbourg he led its church until his death.

He revised the book again and again, in Latin and in French. His French version of 1541 is a landmark of French prose. The final Latin edition of 1559 has four books and eighty chapters. This lesson describes Calvin's teaching as Calvin's, in his own terms.

full.text: Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid Wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves. But as these are connected together by many ties, it is not easy to determine which of the two precedes and gives birth to the other.
full.author: John Calvin
full.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapter 1

full.text: On the other hand, it is evident that man never attains to a true self-knowledge until he have previously contemplated the face of God, and come down after such contemplation to look into himself.
full.author: John Calvin
full.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapter 1

full.html: The argument runs both ways. Looking at our own weakness, Calvin says, drives us to look for God; and only by comparing ourselves with God's goodness do we see ourselves truly. The whole book unfolds from this pairing.

head: Key idea
Calvin's teaching (as he states it)
rows: God is known dimly in creation, and clearly in the Bible, which is the final authority for faith.
God rules and cares for everything that happens.
Since Adam, human nature is deeply damaged by sin, and cannot save itself.
People are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ, not by earning it; good works follow as fruit.
God has chosen from eternity those who will be saved. Calvin calls this a comfort to believers and warns against prying into it.
The true church is where the Word is preached and the two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, are rightly given.
Rulers are appointed by God for order and justice and should be obeyed, though lesser magistrates may resist a tyrant, and God must be obeyed before any human ruler.
full.cap: Main teachings of the Institutes (our summary).

full.title: Counting the chapters
full.q: The four books of the 1559 Institutes have 18, 17, 25 and 20 chapters. How many chapters in all, and which book is longest?
steps: Book III, on faith and the Christian life, has the most: 25.
full.a: 80 chapters; Book III is the longest.

full.html: Calvin's teaching won wide followings and fierce opponents. Catholic theologians rejected his views on the church, the sacraments and justification. Among Protestants, Lutherans differed with him on the Lord's Supper, and from about 1600 the followers of Jacobus Arminius disputed his teaching on election, a debate that continues in churches today. Calvin's Geneva has been admired for its schools, its care for refugees and its orderly church, and criticized for its strict control of private life; the burning of the anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus in 1553, which Calvin supported, has troubled readers from his own century on.

His influence reached far beyond theology. Reformed churches spread to Scotland (with John Knox), the Netherlands, Hungary and France (the Huguenots), and to England and New England with the Puritans. Historians still debate how much Calvinism shaped ideas of work, education and self-government in those lands.
Treating "Calvinism" as Calvin's teaching only about predestination. That is one doctrine among many in the Institutes, which Calvin placed late in Book III and handled with caution.

deep.html: Calvin was trained as a humanist: his first book was a commentary on Seneca. He brought the humanist habits of going back to original sources, reading Greek and Hebrew, and writing clearly. The Institutes quotes Augustine more than any other writer after the Bible, and also cites Plato, Cicero and Seneca.

items: Calvin says knowing God and knowing ourselves depend on each other. Do you think self-knowledge needs something beyond the self?
How should a community balance shared rules with individual freedom of conscience?
What do people owe their rulers, and when, if ever, may they resist?

deep.html: Earlier on this ladder, Augustine and Aquinas wrote the great systematic accounts of Christian teaching Calvin read and argued with. Later, Pascal (a Catholic writing against Calvin's Jesuit opponents and sometimes accused of being too close to Calvin) and Locke (on toleration and government) take up the questions he raised.

questions: Calvin says true wisdom is knowing God and knowing ourselves. What do you think true wisdom is?
Why do you think Calvin kept rewriting his book for twenty-three years?
Calvin asked the King of France to stop persecuting people for their beliefs. Why is freedom of religion important?
People disagreed fiercely about Calvin's ideas. How can people who disagree about deep questions still live together peacefully?
care: This lesson describes Calvin's religious teaching respectfully, as his own views, and gives the main points on which other Christians and later critics disagreed. It does not argue for or against any faith.
